prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The development of state-of-the-art text-to-image (T2I) generative models is currently gated by prohibitive computational costs and massive dataset requirements. The core bottleneck lies in the architecture of Diffusion Transformers: the computational cost scales with the input sequence length (the number of image patches). While reducing the sequence length via patch masking is a known optimization technique, current approaches fail to scale effectively. Existing methods suffer drastic performance degradation when masking ratios exceed moderate levels because they drop patches at the input layer, permanently removing unobserved regions from the model's context. Consequently, training large-scale models remains accessible only to entities with massive GPU clusters and proprietary data.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the performance collapse observed at high masking ratios is not due to the reduction in token count itself, but rather the loss of global semantic information caused by "blind" masking at the input stage.

We propose that if image patches are allowed to communicate and fuse information *before* being masked, the surviving patches can act as compressed representatives of the entire image. By "deferring" the masking step until after a lightweight mixing phase, we believe we can train Diffusion Transformers with extremely high masking ratios (processing significantly fewer tokens) without compromising the model's ability to learn global structure and semantics.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose an end-to-end training pipeline designed to minimize computational overhead while maximizing representational power. The approach consists of three key conceptual components:

**1. Deferred Masking via Patch-Mixing**
Instead of the standard practice of masking raw image patches immediately, we will introduce a "Patch-Mixer" module.
*   **Mechanism:** All input patches will first pass through this lightweight, shallow transformer module. Its sole purpose is to allow information flow between patches.
*   **The "Deferral":** Masking is applied *after* this mixing stage. Because the patches have already interacted, the non-masked tokens passed to the main backbone will contain embedded semantic information regarding the masked (dropped) regions.
*   **Benefit:** This allows the heavy backbone model to process a vastly reduced sequence length while still maintaining a global understanding of the image content.

**2. Sparse Backbone Architecture**
To further decouple parameter count from training cost, we will modify the main Diffusion Transformer backbone.
*   **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE):** We will replace standard feedforward layers with MoE layers using expert-choice routing. This allows us to scale up the total model parameters significantly without increasing the FLOPs required per training step, as only a subset of experts is activated for each token.
*   **Layer-wise Scaling:** We will implement variable width across the network depth, allocating more parameters to deeper layers where visual features are more complex, optimizing the parameter-to-compute ratio.

**3. Synthetic Data Integration**
To address the data bottleneck, we aim to investigate the utility of synthetic data in a micro-budget context. We will train the model using a hybrid of publicly available real images and synthetic captions/images, testing the intuition that synthetic data can serve as a sufficient signal for high-fidelity generation when real data is scarce.

## Expected Contribution
We aim to democratize the training of large-scale generative models by proving that high-fidelity diffusion models can be trained on a "micro-budget." Theoretically, this work will demonstrate that the information redundancy in image patches can be efficiently compressed via deferred masking, rendering the processing of full image sequences unnecessary during training. Practically, this will result in a training pipeline that achieves competitive performance with an order-of-magnitude reduction in diverse computational costs compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a training pipeline focused on "micro-budget" resources to evaluate the effectiveness of deferred patch masking and synthetic data integration in diffusion transformers.

*   **Model Architectures:**
    *   **MicroDiT (Main):** 1.16 billion parameter sparse transformer.
    *   **Base Architectures:** Variants of Diffusion Transformer (DiT), specifically DiT-Tiny/2 (for ablations) and DiT-XL/2 (for large scale).
    *   **Patch Size:** 2.
    *   **Sparsity:** Utilized 8-expert Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) blocks replacing every alternate transformer block.
    *   **Key Mechanism:** Deferred Masking (masking patches *after* processing with a lightweight patch-mixer).
    *   **Patch-Mixer:** A lightweight transformer with a few layers used to fuse embeddings of individual patches before masking.

*   **Training Configuration:**
    *   **Optimizer:** AdamW with cosine learning rate decay and high weight decay.
    *   **Masking Ratio:** Primarily 75% for large-scale experiments.
    *   **Training Schedule (Large Scale):** Total 305,000 steps.
        *   Phase 1: 250,000 steps at $256 \times 256$ resolution.
        *   Phase 2: 55,000 steps at $512 \times 512$ resolution.
    *   **Ablation Schedule:** 60,000 steps (for small-scale comparisons).
    *   **Hardware:** $8 \times$ H100 GPU node (cost estimated at \$30/hour).

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Real Images (~22M pairs):** Conceptual Captions (CC12M), Segment Anything (SA1B), TextCaps.
    *   **Synthetic Images (~15M pairs):** JourneyDB, DiffusionDB.
    *   **Combined Dataset (Large Scale):** 37M image-text pairs (Real + Synthetic).
    *   **Synthetic Scaling Dataset:** Diffusion1B (subset used: ~490M to 500M images).
    *   **Small-Scale Ablation Dataset:** "cifar-captions" (subsampled images of ten CIFAR-10 classes from COYO-700M).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **FID-30K:** Fréchet Inception Distance using Inception-v3 on 30,000 samples from COCO 2014 validation set.
    *   **GenEval:** Compositional image generation benchmark (accuracy).
    *   **Clip-FID & Clip-Score:** Metrics using CLIP model.
    *   **Human Preference:** Pairwise comparison on "Image Quality" and "Alignment with Prompt".

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   Dall-E 2, GigaGAN, Imagen.
    *   Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 2.1.
    *   Würstchen.
    *   PixArt-$\alpha$.
    *   Internal baselines: Naive masking, MaskDiT, Model downscaling.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Data Block 1: Quantitative Evaluation of Large-Scale Models**
*Comparison of the proposed MicroDiT against state-of-the-art text-to-image models regarding parameters, efficiency, and generation quality.*

| Model | Params | Sampling steps | Open source | Training images | 8xH100 GPU days | FID-30K (Lower is better) | GenEval (Higher is better) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Dall-E.2 | 6.50B | - | No | 650M | 2083.2 | 10.39 | 0.52 |
| GigaGAN | 1.01B | 1 | No | 980M | 239.1 | 9.09 | - |
| ImageN | 3.00B | - | No | 860M | 356.6 | 7.27 | - |
| Stable-Diffusion-2.1 | 0.86B | 50 | Yes | 3900M | 416.5 | 9.12 | 0.50 |
| Stable-Diffusion-1.5 | 0.86B | 50 | Yes | 4800M | 312.5 | 11.18 | 0.43 |
| Würstchen | 0.99B | 60 | Yes | 1420M | 51.2 | 23.60 | - |
| PixArt-$\alpha$ | 0.61B | 20 | Yes | 25M (inc. 10M proprietary) | 37.6 | 7.32 | 0.48 |
| **MicroDiT (Ours)** | **1.16B** | **30** | **Yes** | **37M** | **2.6** | **12.66** | **0.46** |

**Data Block 2: Ablation Study on Deferred Masking Components**
*Impact of specific design choices on performance metrics at a 75% masking ratio (Dataset: cifar-captions).*

| Configuration | FID (Lower is better) | Clip-FID (Lower is better) | Clip-score (Higher is better) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Out-of-box | 8.82 | 5.03 | 26.72 |
| Higher weight decay | 8.38 | 4.90 | 27.00 |
| Sigma distribution | 8.49 | 4.93 | 27.47 |
| Larger patch-mixer | 7.40 | 4.57 | 27.79 |
| Higher learning rate | 7.09 | 4.10 | 28.24 |

**Data Block 3: Human Preference Win Rates (Synthetic-Only Model)**
*Win percentages of the MicroDiT model trained solely on 490M synthetic images against open-source baselines.*

| Opposing Model | Quality Win % (Ours) | Alignment Win % (Ours) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Stable-Diffusion-1.5 | 47.3 | 55.8 |
| Stable-Diffusion-2.1 | 53.8 | 51.3 |
| Würstchen | 47.6 | 53.3 |
| PixArt-$\alpha$ | 48.5 | 45.2 |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Masking Strategy Effectiveness**
*   **Observation:** Naive masking caused significant performance degradation at high masking ratios. For example, at a 75% masking ratio, naive masking resulted in an FID of 16.5, whereas the deferred masking approach achieved an FID of 5.03 (much closer to the unmasked baseline FID of 3.79).
*   **Observation:** The MaskDiT approach (masking with autoencoding loss) showed only marginal improvement over naive masking at high ratios because it still dropped patches at the input layer.
*   **Observation:** Deferred masking maintained stable FID, Clip-FID, and Clip-scores up to 75% masking, whereas naive and MaskDiT metrics deteriorated sharply after 50%.
*   **Observation:** Computational cost (ExaFLOPs) decreased linearly with masking ratio for all methods. Deferred masking incurred nearly identical computational costs to MaskDiT.

**Comparison with Alternative Efficiency Methods**
*   **Observation:** Increasing patch size from 2 to 4 (equivalent to 75% reduction in sequence length) resulted in worse performance compared to 75% deferred masking.
    *   *Data point:* Patch size 4 achieved FID 9.38, Clip-FID 6.31, Clip-score 26.70.
    *   *Data point:* Deferred masking achieved FID 7.09, Clip-FID 4.10, Clip-score 28.24.
*   **Observation:** Under IsoFLOPs conditions (identical training time and FLOPs), deferred masking outperformed model downscaling (reducing network size) across metrics until extremely high masking ratios (>75%). At >87.5% masking, downscaling became superior due to excessive information loss in masking.

**Ablation Findings**
*   **Observation:** Random masking (block size $b=1$) outperformed block masking ($b=2, 4, 8$). Performance degraded as block size increased.
*   **Observation:** Layer-wise scaling (increasing width in deeper layers) outperformed constant-width baselines.
*   **Observation:** Adding Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers with limited training steps (60K) showed negligible FID change (6.92 vs 6.98), likely due to expert routing requiring more samples. However, in large-scale training (305K steps), removing MoE layers degraded Zero-shot FID-30K from 12.7 to 13.7.
*   **Observation:** Increasing the dimensionality of the latent space hurt performance in the micro-budget setting.

**Dataset and Scale Findings**
*   **Observation:** Training on a combined dataset (22M Real + 15M Synthetic) yielded images that humans preferred 3x more than a model trained on Real images only (22M), despite both models having nearly identical automated FID and GenEval scores.
*   **Observation:** Scaling the synthetic dataset to 490M images (training on synthetic only) further improved the GenEval score from 0.46 to 0.52 compared to the 37M combined model.
*   **Observation:** In human trials, the 490M synthetic-only model was preferred over the 37M combined model in at least 68% of evaluations for both image quality and alignment.

**Final Model Performance**
*   **Observation:** The final MicroDiT model (1.16B parameters) was trained in 2.6 days on a single $8 \times$ H100 machine for a total economical cost of $1,890.
*   **Observation:** This cost was $118 \times$ lower than Stable Diffusion models and $14 \times$ lower than PixArt-$\alpha$ ($28,400).
*   **Observation:** On the color attribution task in GenEval, the model outperformed Stable-Diffusion-XL-turbo and PixArt-$\alpha$.
*   **Observation:** The model achieved near-perfect accuracy on single-object generation tasks.

[AVAILABLE FIGURES]
### AVAILABLE FIGURES LIST
Item 1:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Comparing performance of patch masking strategies. Using a lightweight patch-mixer before patch masking in our deferred masking approach significantly improves image generation performance over baseline masking strategies.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 2:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. Ablating individual design choices in deferred masking, spanning from training hyperparameters to patch masking strategies.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Compressing patch sequence to reduce computational cost. As the training cost of diffusion transformers is proportional to sequence size, i.e., number of patches, it is desirable to reduce the sequence size without degrading performance. It can be achieved by a) using larger patches, b) naively masking a fraction of patches at random, or c) using MaskDiT [91] that combines naive masking with an additional autoencoding objective. We find all three approaches lead to significant degradation in image generation performance, especially at high masking ratios. To alleviate this issue, we propose a straightforward deferred masking strategy, where we mask patches after they are processed by a patch-mixer. Our approach is analogous to naive masking in all aspects except the use of patch-mixer. In comparison to MaskDiT, our approach doesn’t require optimizing any surrogate objectives and has nearly identical computational costs.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_1.png
  - Caption: Figure 1. Qualitative evaluation of the image generation capabilities of our model (512 → 512 image resolution). Our model is trained in 2.6 days on a single 8→H100 machine (amounting to only $1,890 in GPU cost) without any proprietary or billion image dataset. In (a)-(c) we examine diverse style generation capabilities using prompt ‘Image of an astronaut riding a horse in style’, with following styles: Origami, Pixel art, Line art. In (d) we compare training cost and fidelity, measured using FID [29] for zero-shot image generation on COCO [43] dataset, of all models. We provide an extensive collection of samples generated by our model in Figure 15-28 in the Appendix.
--------------------------------------------------

Figures are located in the figures/ directory and should be referenced appropriately in the paper using standard \includegraphics commands.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\

  \end{tabular}
  \caption{Results.   Ours is better.}
  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

  \centering
  \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{0.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
   %\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{egfigure.eps}

   \caption{Example of caption.
   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}{0.68\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.28\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Training state-of-the-art text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models currently requires exorbitant computational resources, often exceeding tens of thousands of GPU hours. This high cost creates a significant barrier to entry, concentrating development within a few resource-rich organizations. The primary computational bottleneck in modern architectures—specifically Diffusion Transformers (DiTs)—is the quadratic or linear dependence of the transformer's cost on the input sequence size (the number of image patches).

Existing methods to reduce this cost, such as naive patch masking, fail to scale effectively. When masking ratios exceed 50%, performance degrades drastically because the transformer completely loses access to the information contained in the masked patches at the input layer. Furthermore, alternative approaches like MaskDiT require complex auxiliary losses (e.g., reconstruction objectives) and hyperparameter tuning, yet still suffer from information loss at the input stage. We need a training methodology that drastically reduces the effective sequence length without discarding the semantic context required for learning global image structure.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a **Deferred Masking** strategy to decouple computational cost from information retention. Our core hypothesis is that by preprocessing *all* image patches using a lightweight, small-scale "patch-mixer" *before* applying the masking operation, the surviving non-masked patches will embed semantic information about the entire image.

This approach will allow us to train Diffusion Transformers at significantly higher masking ratios (up to 75%) without the performance degradation associated with naive masking. By integrating this with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers and synthetic data utilization, we aim to build a "MicroDiT" architecture that achieves competitive generation quality on a micro-budget, effectively democratizing large-scale diffusion training.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Diffusion Training
We will adopt the standard diffusion formulation where data $( \pmb { x } , \pmb { c } ) \sim \mathcal { D }$ represents the image and caption pairs. We model the forward and reverse processes using the probability flow ODE:
$$ \mathrm { d } \pmb { x } = - \dot { \sigma } ( t ) \sigma ( t ) \nabla _ { \pmb { x } } \log p ( \pmb { x } ; \sigma ( t ) ) \mathrm { d } t $$
where $\sigma(t)$ is the time-dependent noise standard deviation. Our objective is to learn the denoiser $F_\theta$ to approximate the score $\nabla _ { \pmb { x } } \log p ( \pmb { x } ; \sigma ( t ) )$.

### 2. Deferred Patch Masking Strategy
Unlike standard approaches that mask raw patches immediately, we will insert a lightweight **Patch-Mixer** ($M_\phi$) prior to the masking step. The pipeline is defined as follows:

1.  **Patch Extraction:** The input image $\pmb{x}$ is tokenized into a sequence of patches.
2.  **Patch Mixing:** The full sequence is processed by $M_\phi$, a small transformer comprising only a few layers and a fraction of the backbone's parameter count. This allows information flow between all patches.
3.  **Masking:** We apply a binary mask $m$ to the output of the patch-mixer.
4.  **Backbone Processing:** Only the unmasked tokens are fed into the heavy backbone transformer $F_\theta$.

The training loss is formulated as:
$$ \mathcal { L } = \mathbb { E } _ { ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { c } ) \sim \mathcal { D } } \mathbb { E } _ { \pmb { \epsilon } \sim \mathcal { N } ( \mathbf { 0 } , \sigma ( t ) ^ { 2 } \mathbf { I } ) } | | F _ { \theta } ( M _ { \phi } ( \pmb { x } + \pmb { \epsilon } ; \sigma ( t ) , \pmb { c } ) \odot ( 1 - m ) ; \sigma ( t ) , \pmb { c } ) - \pmb { x } \odot ( 1 - m ) | | _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } $$

Here, we compute the loss only on the unmasked patches. Crucially, we do **not** use auxiliary reconstruction losses (like MaskDiT), simplifying the optimization landscape. During inference, no masking is applied.

### 3. Backbone Architecture Improvements
To maximize parameter efficiency and expressivity, the backbone $F_\theta$ will incorporate specific architectural advancements:

*   **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE):** We will implement sparse transformer blocks using MoE. Specifically, we will use **Expert-Choice Routing**, where experts select the tokens they process. This avoids the load-balancing auxiliary losses required by token-choice routing. We will replace every alternate transformer block with an 8-expert MoE block.
*   **Layer-wise Scaling:** We will linearly increase the hidden layer dimension (width) of the transformer blocks as the depth increases. This allocates more parameters to deeper layers, which are hypothesized to process more complex visual features.
*   **Activation Functions:** We will utilize SwiGLU activations instead of GELU, aligning with recent findings in Large Language Model (LLM) training.

### 4. Training Configuration and Noise Scheduling
*   **Noise Distribution:** We will shift the log-normal noise distribution to better align with high-resolution signal-to-noise ratios. We plan to set the distribution parameters to $\ln ( \sigma ) \sim \mathcal { N } ( -0.6, 1.2 )$.
*   **Optimization:** We will use the AdamW optimizer with cosine learning rate decay and high weight decay.
*   **Two-Phase Training:**
    1.  **Masked Pretraining:** Training with the deferred masking strategy at high ratios (e.g., 75%).
    2.  **Unmasked Finetuning:** A short duration of unmasked training to align the train-test distribution of sequence sizes and remove potential artifacts.

### 5. Data Strategy
We will not rely solely on massive real-world datasets. Instead, we will construct a training pipeline that heavily utilizes **synthetic images** (e.g., from existing diffusion models) combined with available real datasets. We hypothesize that scaling the synthetic dataset size is sufficient for high-quality generation, allowing us to bypass the need for proprietary billion-scale real image datasets.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Algorithmic Innovation:** The introduction of Deferred Masking will theoretically demonstrate that masking in diffusion transformers is a design choice, not a fundamental constraint, and that global context can be preserved efficiently via a patch-mixer.
2.  **Cost Efficiency:** We expect to reduce the training cost of billion-parameter scale diffusion models by over an order of magnitude compared to state-of-the-art baselines, making training feasible on a "micro-budget."
3.  **Data Insight:** We aim to establish that micro-budget training pipelines can achieve competitive performance using significantly smaller, synthetically augmented datasets (approx. 37M images) rather than requiring billions of real images.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
